---
title: "Reliable Notifications Without Double-Sending"
description: "Challenging system-design interview scenario: formal guarantee, failures, and an original implementation."
---

## Interview challenge

You must send account alerts. The message broker delivers an event, the notification worker calls an email/SMS provider, and then the worker crashes before acknowledging the event. The broker retries. Does your design send the user another email?

The crucial distinction is **at-least-once event delivery** versus **exactly-once external side effects**.

## Identify the separate boundaries

1. An event is committed to durable storage or a broker.
2. A worker receives the event and may retry.
3. The worker calls the external notification provider.
4. The provider accepts or rejects the request.
5. The worker acknowledges the broker message.

The worker can crash between any two stages. A successful provider call can have an unknown outcome from the worker's perspective, just as with the payment case.

## An idempotency design

Assign each logical notification a stable ID derived from the source event ID and notification type. Persist a per-recipient delivery state. Repeated broker deliveries should not create new logical notification records.

~~~ts
const gate = new IdempotencyGate<string>();
const send = async () => 'provider-message-123';
const first = gate.run('event7:email:alice','template-v1',send);
const second = gate.run('event7:email:alice','template-v1',send);
~~~

The core example deduplicates calls **inside one process**, while [SequencedInbox](../lab/src/core.ts) demonstrates ordering for dependent events. A real solution uses an atomic DB unique key or consumer inbox and preferably a provider-supplied idempotency reference.

## The unsolved hard edge case

If the provider sends the email and the network response is lost, you may not know whether the email was delivered. A local SQL transaction cannot atomically commit with an arbitrary email provider. If the provider offers an idempotency key or a lookup API, use it; otherwise acknowledge the possibility of duplicate delivery, and design business and UX semantics accordingly.

Do not assert 'exactly-once email' merely because your broker advertises exactly-once processing semantics within its own infrastructure.

## Additional decisions

Per-recipient rate limits prevent a notification storm; preferences and unsubscribe status must be checked at the correct authoritative moment. Keep sensitive content out of long-lived message payloads when practical. Use retries with jitter and maximum attempts, with dead-letter handling and monitoring for permanently failed notifications.

## Interview follow-ups

- What if a fraud alert and a marketing email share a retry queue? Separate priority and admission policies so low-value bulk email cannot delay security notifications.
- Can notification order matter? For account state messages, yes; enforce per-recipient or per-aggregate ordering when required.
- What does a deduplication retention window mean? After eviction, an old replay may be treated as new; align retention with the broker's replay horizon.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
\#\mathrm{LogicalNotifications}(eventId,recipient,type)\leq1.
$$

This is an **application-level idempotency goal**. It is weaker than a claim that an external recipient observes no duplicate delivery under all possible failures.

**References:** [Microsoft: Idempotent Consumer](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/idempotent-consumer) and [Competing Consumers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/competing-consumers).
